newsitem.title: GERMANY: Tietmeyer stresses importance of all EMU criteria.
newsitem.headline: Tietmeyer stresses importance of all EMU criteria.

text.p: Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said on Thursday the economic convergence criteria required for launching the European single currency in 1999 must be seen as a single unit and not taken individually.

In the text of a speech, Tietmeyer said all the convergence criteria for launching the single currency -- stable inflation, membership of the ERM, currency stability, solid state finances and low long term interest rates -- were important.

"These criteria form a unit and are not to be separated. Participating countries must fulfil these criteria in their substance on the appointed day and -- more importantly -- beyond," he said. The speech was released ahead of delivery at an economic conference in Erfurt.

The single currency is due for launch on January 1, 1999, and would-be participants are required to meet economic targets on interest and exchange rates, inflation, budget deficits and public borrowing.
But the wording of some of the criteria allows room for some flexibility in defining the exact goals.

Tietmeyer's apparent hardline approach follows remarks made by fellow Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke earlier this week which seemed to indicate flexibility in interpreting the Maastricht convergence criteria.
Welteke said that the flexibility in the interpretation of the entry criteria was greater than described but warned that it was nonetheless limited and could not be used arbitrarily.
Bundesbank board member Edgar Meister took a similar line, calling on the European Monetary Institute and European Commission to define the criteria as precisely as possible.
But council members Reimut Jochimsen and Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher made clear that they believed the criteria should be interpreted as strictly as possible.

Tietmeyer reaffirmed the importance of strict fiscal discipline in the run-up to European monetary union and thereafter and his belief that immediate sanctions should be imposed if countries stepped out of line.

The Maastricht Treaty has set the reference value for nations' budget deficits at three percent of gross domestic product and calls for national debt to be no more than 60 percent of GDP -- both targets which Germany missed last year.
"The currency union can only start with a durable basis. Anything else would be irresponsible," he said.
"I continue to believe that semi-automatically effective sanctions -- as the German side has suggested -- are important in the case of an EMU country breaching fiscal discipline," he said.

Tietmeyer said sanctions might not be enforced if transgressions were temporary but said the burden of proof would lie with errant countries to convince other member states that the breach was an exception.
The alternative scenario, imposing sanctions on the basis of a majority vote, was "not particularly effective," he said.
Tietmeyer noted budgetary conditions in most European countries had worsened since the Maastricht Treaty was signed in 1992.

"Germany is no exception. The necessary economic rebuilding of the new (eastern) German states certainly played a special role. But that does not excuse or justify a high public debt in the long term," Tietmeyer said.
The Bundesbank president added, however, that many European countries were making strenuous efforts to reduce deficits.
